title: Clockless delay-insensitive memory interface
idea: MINIFY clocking to zero: replace the DDR clock, DLLs and training with 1-of-4 delay-insensitive handshake coding between DRAM and host, so the I/O idles at zero dynamic power.
why: Interface idle power (DLL/PLL is a large share of DRAM standby I/O): claims 30-50% lower interface power and no training time.

title: Optically bistable microrings buffer packets inside photonic interposers
idea: Worsen: convert every optical packet to electrons and park it in DRAM for microseconds. Flip: use carrier- or thermo-optically bistable silicon microrings, where a holding beam keeps each ring in one of two transmission states, as nanosecond photonic latches that buffer packets in the optical domain.
why: Data movement: avoids the O-E-O plus DRAM round trip (~10-20 pJ/bit) for switch and link buffers; no capacitor, small capacity.

title: Origami memory: fold a flex ribbon of dies over compute
idea: Rearrange a planar layout into a fold: bond thinned memory dies to a parylene or polyimide flex with litho-patterned 5 um copper traces, then fold it accordion-style so the dies stack above the compute die while their wiring runs around the folds instead of through the silicon.
why: TSV-free 3D stacking with <5 mm links (fact 6), each die keeping its own traces; flex fabrication is standard in university cleanrooms.

title: Foldable-phone Z-fold flex memory stack
idea: Foldable phones bend circuits on polyimide. Mount thinned DRAM dies along one long polyimide flex (cured ≤350 C) carrying fine Cu traces, test every die flat, then Z-fold the strip accordion-style into a stack. Tier-to-tier signals travel over the folds instead of TSVs.
why: No TSV processing, and each die is tested before folding, which gives known-good stacks. It trades some wire length for 30-50% lower stacking cost.

title: Femtosecond-laser-written waveguides inside glass interposers
idea: Substitute copper interposer RDL with optical waveguides written in 3D inside a fused-silica interposer by femtosecond-laser index modification, evanescently coupled to grating ports on the GPU and HBM base die; waveguides cross in 3D without crosstalk, collapsing many routing layers into one glass volume.
why: Fact 5: interposer hop from ~3-4 pJ/bit toward ~1 pJ/bit, and HBM can sit 20-50 mm away, breaking the shoreline limit on stack count.

title: Lid-as-interposer: the heat spreader carries memory signals
idea: Substitute the silicon interposer with the package lid: a copper/AlN ceramic lid with embedded multilayer redistribution bonds face-down onto GPU and HBM tops and carries die-to-die signals, while the organic substrate below handles only power and external I/O.
why: Fact 6/5: deletes a >2,500 mm2 silicon interposer, frees the bottom side for power, and pulls heat out of taller stacks directly.

title: Origami flex interposer folds memory stacks around the processor
idea: Substitute the flat interposer with a 2 um-line polyimide flex bonded at the GPU edges and folded up and over, so HBM stacks mount on vertical walls and above the GPU, tripling the number of stacks within 5 mm of the die edge.
why: Shoreline limit (Facts 5/6): ~3x more stacks per processor without longer wires; memory capacity per accelerator up 2-3x.

title: Laser-drilled glass interposer with aerosol-jet silver wiring
idea: Substitute the foundry silicon interposer with a 300 um glass sheet: a UV picosecond laser drills through-glass vias and an aerosol-jet printer writes 10 um silver traces and polyimide dielectric layer by layer; a 10-person shop runs it with two tools and a curing oven.
why: Capital intensity: interposer tooling from a >$100M line to <$2M, with enough density for 512-1024-bit LPDDR buses next to a processor.

title: Poor man's HBM on commercial HDI substrates
idea: Substitute the silicon interposer with a commercial mSAP HDI board (15 um lines) carrying bare LPDDR5X dies flip-chipped within 3 mm of an FPGA/ASIC, running a 1024-bit bus at a modest 2-3 Gb/s per pin.
why: Cost per bit and capital: roughly HBM2-class bandwidth at LPDDR cost without TSVs or scarce CoWoS capacity.

title: Double-sided interposer with HBM mounted directly beneath the GPU
idea: Combine double-sided module assembly with 2.5D packaging: mount HBM stacks on the underside of a thin interposer directly under the GPU, connected by ~100 um through-interposer vias instead of 5-10 mm lateral wires, with the package substrate cavity-milled to receive them.
why: Data movement and interposer area: 50x shorter links (~0.5 pJ/bit), 8+ stacks without beachfront limits, ~40% smaller interposer.

title: MRI-style cryostat with superconducting interposer for memory links
idea: Adapted from the MRI magnet and superconducting-wire industry: the accelerator+DRAM module runs in a 77 K closed-cycle cryostat on an interposer with YBCO high-temperature superconducting traces. Links become nearly lossless, and DRAM leakage falls by orders of magnitude.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and refresh (fact 3): near-zero resistive link loss and 100x+ retention at 77 K; this works only if cryocooler overhead stays below the energy saved.

title: Interposer that remembers: BEOL non-volatile memory inside it
idea: Eliminate the interposer's passivity: the ~2500 mm2 silicon interposer (65 nm-class, cheap, U.S.-fabbable) becomes an active interposer with BEOL MRAM or HZO FeRAM arrays and simple peripheral CMOS under and between chiplets, stacking 3-4 BEOL array layers.
why: Adds ~5-8 GB of NV capacity 1-2 mm from compute without extra dies, packages or EUV, reusing area that is today pure wiring, at ~0.5 pJ/bit.

title: Copying: passive optical splitters broadcast one weight read to many chips
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: in data-parallel inference every accelerator holds an identical copy of the weights. Instead, one memory node reads each weight block once and broadcasts it in lockstep to all accelerators through cheap passive 1:16 PON fiber splitters (mass-produced telecom parts). (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less: replicated weight storage falls by up to 16x, freeing HBM for KV cache, using existing telecom optics capacity.

title: Si: die-agnostic DDR5 buffer builds RDIMMs from any surplus die
idea: Put a silicon bridge buffer (extended RCD plus data buffers) on a standard DDR5 RDIMM that speaks JEDEC DDR5 to the host but drives LPDDR4X/LPDDR5, DDR4 or downbinned dies behind it, translating timing and bank structure, so modules can be assembled from whatever DRAM die is in surplus.
why: Usable supply with host interface unchanged: mobile and legacy DRAM inventories and mature DDR4 lines become server DDR5 capacity, adding several % of bits to the tightest market segment.

title: Reticle-stitched mega-DRAM wafer-bonded to logic
idea: MAGNIFY die size by stitching the DRAM array across 4+ reticles into one ~3,000 mm^2 die, bonded wafer-on-wafer to a logic wafer, with no dicing, no package I/O and no TSVs; row/column redundancy absorbs defects.
why: Packaging cost and data movement: removes the PHY and bumps; claims ~0.05 pJ/bit and terabytes per second per die.

title: Contactless capacitive stacking through 1 um dies, link errors folded in
idea: Replace data TSVs with capacitive couplers across dies thinned to ~1 um: the coupled signal is marginal (raw link BER ~1e-3), but it is simply added to the 1% cell error budget and corrected by the same code. Dies join by oxide-oxide fusion bonding, with only a few large vias for power.
why: Removes most TSV area and yield tax (fact 6: 3x area, -20-30% yield); oxide-only bonding is cheaper and more defect-tolerant than Cu-Cu hybrid bonding.

title: Memory dust: fluidic self-assembled micro-DRAM chiplets
idea: MINIFY chiplets to ~0.5 mm^2 (128 Mb each) and place thousands of them into etched receptor sites on the compute wafer by shape-matched fluidic self-assembly, borrowing microLED mass-transfer methods.
why: Data movement and yield: memory is sprinkled within ~1 mm of every core, and known-good tiny dies yield >99%.

title: Pinless DRAM die fed data by light through its backside
idea: Po: memory with no pins. A VCSEL array in the package lid shines modulated light onto Ge photodiode and micro-LED tiles on each thinned DRAM die's backside, so the bumps carry only power and ground and each die exchanges data with the logic die through free space.
why: Removes signal TSVs and microbumps (HBM TSV tax) and decouples die count from bump field; targets ~0.5 pJ/bit and 2x more dies per package footprint.

title: Uncut wafer-scale DRAM slab with redundancy routing fabric
idea: Box: 1T1C DRAM x standard x standard x on-wafer mesh network with spare-tile routing x whole 300 mm wafer x no dicing. The entire DRAM wafer serves as one memory, with a reconfigurable mesh that routes around bad tiles, face-to-face bonded to a wafer-scale compute or optical I/O wafer.
why: Packaging cost and data movement: no dicing, bumping or per-die packaging; ~1-2 TB per wafer at ~0.3 pJ/bit; yield handled by redundancy instead of scrap.

title: Self-healing links with spare lanes and field remap
idea: MAGNIFY lane redundancy to ~10% spares with a base-die crossbar that keeps checking bump and TSV margins in service and retires links degraded by electromigration on the fly.
why: Lifetime and yield: packages repair their own wires instead of failing; claims 2x interconnect lifetime.

title: Sous-vide chef: memory held isothermal at a constant 125 C
idea: Sous-vide works because the temperature never changes: instead of fighting heat, on-die heaters hold the memory stack at a constant 125 C at all times, so it never thermally cycles, and refresh and link timing are calibrated once for that single point.
why: Thermal-cycling fatigue of bumps and interposers, the main packaging failure mode, is eliminated; one-temperature tuning recovers margin that wide-range designs waste.

title: Rack-shared scrub appliance replaces per-device heavy decoders
idea: Shift heavy correction to rack scale and hour timescale: long-retention memory devices carry only a light access-path decoder sized for 1% raw BER, while one rack-level appliance with powerful soft decoders sweeps every pool over CXL in low-load hours, rewriting rows before drift pushes errors past 1%. Refresh becomes an hourly network service.
why: Amortizes decoder silicon across hundreds of devices and replaces ms-scale refresh (fact 3) with hourly scrubbing for long-retention cells.

title: Elastomer stamps mass-transfer memory dielets dry, microLED-style
idea: Box: 0.3 mm DRAM dielets x standard x standard x transfer-printed onto RDL x panel x laser release from carrier plus kinetically controlled PDMS stamp mass transfer. Borrowed from microLED fabs, one stamp stroke picks up 10,000 dielets and prints them onto the panel.
why: Water: replaces water-sprayed blade dicing and wet release with laser release and dry transfer, >10x cut; small dielets raise yield and allow fine-grained memory placement.

title: Tin-free joints: sintered copper bonds from domestic copper
idea: Invert 'packages need tin-silver solder': join dies and stacks with sintered copper-nanoparticle paste or direct Cu-Cu thermocompression, using U.S.-mined copper and no tin, silver or indium.
why: The U.S. mines no tin; copper joints remove that import, conduct better, tolerate higher temperatures and reach finer pitch (<20 um) than solder microbumps.

title: Phase transition: transient-liquid-phase bonding stacks DRAM in standard reflow
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transitions: replace scarce hybrid bonders with Cu-Sn transient-liquid-phase bonding in existing OSAT reflow and thermocompression tools. A thin Sn layer melts and converts to high-melting Cu3Sn, so later tiers bond at ~20 um pitch without remelting earlier ones. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital and the tool chokepoint (fact 6): 12-16-high stacks without new hybrid-bonding capacity, at finer pitch than standard microbumps.

title: Prior counteraction: counter-bowed dies for 24-high stacks
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: measure each tier's bonding warpage, then deposit a tuned SiN backside stress film so each thinned die is pre-bowed the opposite way and goes flat at bonding temperature. This removes edge voids in hybrid-bonded 16-24-high stacks.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): aims to recover ~10 of the 20-30 lost yield points and enables 24-high stacks (+50% GB per footprint).

title: Controller-less DRAM: compiler emits cycle-exact raw memory commands
idea: Eliminate the memory controller's queues, reorder logic and refresh scheduler: for static AI graphs the compiler schedules every ACT/RD/WR/REF at cycle level with temperature-guarded margins, and the PHY simply replays the command stream.
why: Controllers cost SoC area/power and add 20-40 ns latency plus variance; deterministic schedules reach >90% bus utilization and return the area to compute or SRAM.

title: Mo: molybdenum-filled TSVs shrink keep-out zones in HBM dies
idea: Fill HBM core-die TSVs with molybdenum (CTE 4.8 ppm/K vs Cu 17, Si 2.6) instead of copper, cutting thermo-mechanical stress so the transistor keep-out zone around each TSV shrinks from ~5-10 um to ~1-2 um and Cu pumping disappears.
why: HBM TSV area tax (fact 6): reclaims ~3-5% core-die area and reduces TSV-related yield loss with the HBM interface unchanged; avoids tungsten fill and its China chokepoint.

title: Moire magnification: printed interference marks enable nanometer roll-to-roll overlay
idea: Print paired gratings of slightly different pitch on each layer of an R2R interposer; their Moire fringes magnify misalignment 100-1000x and cameras feed real-time web registration actuators, enabling 1-2 um lines with ~100 nm overlay.
why: Brings R2R from ~20 um to near-silicon-interposer density for memory fan-out (facts 4, 6) at a fraction of the capex.

title: Li: beta-eucryptite negative-expansion filler stops HBM package warpage
idea: Replace part of the fused-silica filler in mold compound and underfill with beta-eucryptite (LiAlSiO4, CTE ~ -6 ppm/K, from abundant Li, Al, Si) to bring composite CTE to ~3 ppm/K matching silicon, eliminating warpage of 8-12-stack HBM packages.
why: HBM packaging yield and size: warpage limits interposer size and causes bump opens; CTE matching allows more stacks per package and reduces high-purity fused-quartz filler demand.

title: Delay-insensitive self-timed link deletes DRAM DLLs and training
idea: Scarcity: no forwarded clock and no DLL on the DRAM. Send data in a level-encoded dual-rail (1-of-4 transition) code so every symbol carries its own timing; the DRAM side drops DLL/PLL, link training and per-pin deskew.
why: Periphery and idle power (fact 7): DLLs and training logic burn mW per channel at idle; targets 20-30% lower I/O power and near-instant power-state exit.

title: Pupin loading coils make interposer wires distortionless Heaviside lines
idea: Add periodic thin-film CoZrTa-cored inductors along RC-dominated interposer and RDL wires, as Pupin loaded telephone lines, pushing them toward Heaviside's distortionless condition so pulses keep their shape without CTLE/DFE equalizers.
why: Facts 5/6: longer HBM-to-logic reach at low swing without power-hungry equalization, ~30-50% PHY energy savings and more stacks per package; inductor area and loss at GHz are the risk.

title: Checkpoint-in-place: non-volatile HBM ends training checkpoint traffic
idea: Eliminate copying model and optimizer state to storage: on NV-cell HBM, a checkpoint is a metadata flip that seals a copy-on-write page epoch inside the stack, so no checkpoint bytes leave the package; recovery remaps to the last sealed epoch.
why: Big training runs spend ~5-15% of time and huge network/storage bandwidth writing TB-scale checkpoints every ~30 min; removing them raises cluster goodput and deletes the checkpoint storage tier.

title: Coaxial microbumps: two signals per bump, self-shielded
idea: Rearrange the bump: plate a core pillar, coat it with conformal ALD or parylene dielectric, then plate a ring shell, giving a coaxial bump whose core carries one signal and whose shell carries ground or a second signal.
why: Facts 5 and 6: doubles signal density at the same pitch (or allows relaxed pitch), and the shielding cuts crosstalk at 10+ Gb/s; plating and ALD are university staples.

title: Stacked camera-sensor pixel bonding: per-subarray copper ports to logic
idea: Adapted from the pixel-level Cu-Cu hybrid bonding of stacked smartphone image sensors: the DRAM array wafer bonds face-to-face to a logic wafer so each subarray (mat) has its own ~100-wire vertical port. Global I/O routing and shared periphery go away.
why: Periphery 49% of die (fact 7) and data movement: array efficiency toward ~75% and >10x bandwidth at ~0.1 pJ/bit vertical hops.

title: DRAM dies embedded in glass-core substrate cavities under processor
idea: Combine the glass-core package substrates now arriving for AI packages with embedded-die technology: laser-form cavities in the glass core, embed thinned commodity DRAM/LPDDR dies face-up, and connect them with through-glass vias straight up into the GPU bump field so memory sits ~300 um below compute instead of beside it.
why: Data movement and CoWoS/HBM bottleneck: ~1-2 pJ/bit vertical links vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM, no silicon interposer, no TSV stack (avoids 3x HBM area tax), uses commodity DRAM wafers.

title: Latent heat: printed phase-change heat buffers flatten HBM burst temperatures
idea: Screen-print a microencapsulated phase-change composite melting at ~75 C into a lid cavity over the HBM stack so AI burst heat is absorbed at constant temperature, keeping DRAM under the 85 C double-refresh threshold during peaks.
why: Refresh (fact 3): avoids 2x refresh rate in bursts with a cheap printed paste; buffers only seconds-scale transients.

title: Infrared light crosses thinned silicon instead of TSVs
idea: Box: DRAM x standard x Ge photodiode receivers x 1310 nm micro-emitter arrays shining vertically through the dies x thinned Si (transparent at 1.3 um) x no via etch. Signals cross the stack as light through the silicon bulk while power uses a few large peripheral vias.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): removes signal TSV keep-out area and TSV process steps; ~0.5 pJ/bit if emitters are efficient enough.

title: Copper-free capacitive hybrid bond: dielectric bond doubles as signal coupler
idea: Combine oxide-oxide direct bonding with AC-coupled proximity signaling: each die-to-die signal is two overlapping metal plates separated only by the ~0.5 um bond oxide, driven with edge/pulse signaling, so no Cu pads must touch. Only a sparse grid of coarse TSVs carries DC power.
why: HBM stacking yield and alignment: removes Cu dishing/protrusion defects and tightens nothing beyond plate overlap (~+/-1 um) at 2-3 um signal pitch; <0.05 pJ/bit per hop; claims to recover most of the 20-30% stack yield loss.

title: Harvest timing guard bands: cut tRCD and tRP 40% at 1% BER
idea: Shift the access timescale below the worst case: timings set so the slowest cell at the hottest corner never fails are cut ~40%, letting a few slow cells mis-sense and the row code absorb them.
why: ~30-40% lower random-access latency and higher bank throughput, so fewer stacks deliver a target bandwidth.

title: Non-volatile write FIFO in the PHY makes pins persistent
idea: Eliminate cache-flush and fence round trips: put a small ferroelectric-capacitor-backed write queue in the controller PHY and memory base die so a write is durable the moment it crosses the pins; the queue drains to the NV array at leisure and replays after power loss.
why: Persistent-memory software pays ~0.1-1 us per CLWB+SFENCE and doubles traffic with write-ahead logs; durable in-flight path cuts commit latency ~5-10x and removes log write amplification.

title: Electrowetting liquid metal: Galinstan microchannel vias are stress-free and reconfigurable
idea: Fill vertical microchannels with gallium-alloy liquid metal instead of solid Cu, removing CTE stress and keep-out zones; electrowetting electrodes along spare channels move metal plugs to connect or disconnect lanes, giving in-field lane repair.
why: TSV keep-out area and stress-induced yield loss (fact 6); repair without heavy spare-TSV overprovisioning; Ga attack on Al/Cu needs barriers.

title: Bond sense amplifiers straight to compute and delete the PHY
idea: A bit only has to travel ~10 um vertically, so PHY, SerDes, global datapath and pads are overhead, not physics. Hybrid-bond each subarray's local sense-amp column outputs at 1 um pitch directly to registers in the logic die beneath, running millions of unserialized connections at ~200 MHz so the bitline restore charge is essentially the only signaling energy.
why: Removes global I/O wire (often >50% of read energy) and ~10-15% of periphery area; ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM (30x+), bandwidth scales with area instead of shoreline (facts 5, 7).

title: Ultra-wide 200 MHz near-threshold interface with 64k wires per stack
idea: Shift the link's timescale 30x slower and its width 30x wider: with 3 um hybrid bonds a stack exposes 64k data pads clocked at 200 MHz with 0.2 V swing, driven by plain CMOS inverters with no SerDes, DFE, PLL or termination. Bandwidth matches HBM4 while each bit only charges ~20 fF of micron-length wire.
why: Interface energy falls from 3-4 pJ/bit to ~0.03-0.05 pJ/bit (fact 5) and PHY area on base and host dies shrinks ~5x.

title: C: CVD-diamond interleaf shims keep HBM below refresh-doubling heat
idea: Bond 20-30 um polycrystalline CVD diamond layers (1,000-1,500 W/m-K) into HBM/3DS stacks every four dies, with laser-drilled through-diamond vias, so base-die and core-die heat spreads laterally to the lid; the electrical interface is untouched.
why: Refresh (fact 3): above 85 C DRAM must refresh 2x, costing energy and ~10-20% bandwidth; a 10-15 C cooler stack avoids it and lets 16-20-high stacks stay in spec.

title: Resonant interposer bus that recycles line charge every cycle
idea: Ideal: moving a bit costs zero energy. Closest achievable: integrate spiral inductors in the interposer so each memory data line resonates with its own capacitance; bits are encoded as the phase of a resonant swing and 60-80% of the CV2 energy sloshes back each cycle instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Fact 5 and fact 10 voltage floor: link energy falls 3-5x without lowering voltage, beating the CV2 wall by recovery rather than scaling.

title: Power-and-signal superposed TSVs carry DC plus data
idea: Invert 'power and signal need separate vias': each supply TSV carries DC current with a small AC data signal superimposed, separated on each die by an on-die bias-tee (MIM capacitor plus active current source), so power TSVs double as data lanes.
why: Power/ground TSVs are often over half of HBM's TSV count; merging cuts TSV area and keep-out zones ~30-40%, shrinking the HBM TSV area tax.

title: Pupin loading coils make long interposer memory lines distortionless
idea: Adapted from the 1900 telephone loading coil: small thick-metal spiral inductors are added periodically along long memory traces to meet the Heaviside condition (L/C = R/G). A wide slow bus can then stretch 5-10 cm without equalizers.
why: More DRAM dies can sit around a processor (capacity) at near-HBM energy, and power-hungry equalization goes away.

title: Index-list gather engine returns only packed useful words
idea: Ideal: the memory already knows which words you need. Closest achievable: the host sends a list of 4-8 byte indices (embedding rows, sparse nonzeros, KV pages) over the command path, and the base die does bank-parallel fetches and returns densely packed 64 B lines holding only the requested words.
why: Fact 8 and fact 5: sparse and embedding workloads waste 80-95% of transferred bytes; packing cuts interface traffic 5-10x for those patterns.

title: Cheap short-living objects: retired server DDR4 reborn as CXL memory
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Collect, retest and bin them, then mount 8-16 on each CXL Type-3 card built around a 28 nm controller, as a cheap cold tier for KV cache and page cache. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Usable supply: reuses DRAM that already exists, at ~10-20% of new DRAM cost per GB and zero wafer starts.

title: Asymmetry: read-wide, write-narrow memory links for inference
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: inference reads weights and KV cache 10-50x more than it writes. So ~90% of HBM data lanes become one-way DRAM-to-GPU lanes with open-drain low-swing drivers and receiver-only GPU ends, and a narrow bidirectional lane group handles writes and commands.
why: Data movement (fact 5): read lanes need no ODT or driver pairs and have no turnaround, so PHY energy and area per read bit fall ~25-35% and usable bandwidth rises ~10%.

title: Tidal-flow reversible lanes matched to read/write mix
idea: Reversible highway lanes follow the commute. HBM data lanes are split into groups, and the controller sets each group's direction per epoch (for example 15 read : 1 write during decode). This replaces symmetric bidirectional bursts and the turnaround bubbles they cause.
why: LLM inference is about 90% reads. Asymmetric lanes remove turnaround penalties and idle write capacity, for ~10-20% more effective read bandwidth per pin and per TSV.

title: Chef's mise en place: command-less, compiler-scheduled streaming DRAM
idea: A chef preps every ingredient before service: for static AI dataflows, the compiler preloads a whole row schedule into the HBM base die, which then streams data open-loop with no per-access command bus, and the freed command/address pins are repurposed as data lanes.
why: Removes command-bus overhead and scheduling bubbles: ~15% more data pins, ~10% more bandwidth efficiency and lower controller periphery power.

title: Analog pass-through: multilevel NV cells drive PAM4 lanes directly
idea: Eliminate digitization and re-encoding between cell and wire: a 2-bit/cell FeFET array is sensed into four voltage levels that are buffered straight onto a PAM4 lane through an analog mux, and the receiver's slicer performs the only quantization.
why: Removes sense-to-digital-to-serializer stages (~30-40% of read-path energy) and doubles bits per symbol per cell access, while data stays non-volatile.

title: Discarding and recovering: partial-good HBM stacks sold as lower tiers
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: instead of scrapping stacks with one bad tier or weak TSV lanes, fuse out the bad tier or half the lanes in the base die and re-bin the stacks as 8-high or half-width parts for inference cards and edge devices. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: HBM yield (fact 6): turns the 20-30% yield loss into a sellable lower tier, effectively +10-20% usable HBM supply from the same wafers.

title: Urban-mined DRAM dies from retired servers restacked into dense modules
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Chemically decap DDR4 packages from decommissioned servers, retest the harvested dies, thin them and restack 16-32 high with wire-bond or sidewall interconnect into high-capacity modules for a capacity-tier memory product.
why: The dies are already paid for: near-zero die cost lets a module carry 10x the dies at the same price, made domestically from e-waste.

title: Volume holography: printed photopolymer holograms fan one laser to 64 chiplets
idea: Record multiplexed volume holograms in R2R-coated photopolymer film so one input beam diffracts into 64 precisely aimed spots on memory chiplet detectors, distributing broadcast data, clock or optical power across a module with no waveguides.
why: Optical broadcast and laser sharing (fact 5): one source feeds many memory chiplets; holograms are contact-copied at cents; alignment tolerance is the risk.

title: Differential-analyzer revival: ship activations between dies as analog charge
idea: Revive analog computing: between a processing-in-memory die and the logic die, send each 6-bit activation as one analog charge sample per wire per transfer, consumed directly by an analog MAC on the far side with no ADC/DAC pair.
why: Fact 5: ~6x fewer transfers per value and link energy per value near one-bit energy; inference tolerates ~1% analog error, but noise and calibration are the risk.

title: Ballistic transport: printed aligned-nanotube repeaters make long flex memory links
idea: Shear-align printed semiconducting carbon-nanotube films on R2R flex to form short-channel transistor repeaters every few mm along memory interconnect, enabling GHz signaling over 10 cm of flex without silicon.
why: Data movement over printed substrates (fact 5): an active printed interposer at R2R cost; nanotube purity and alignment are high risk.

title: Bond-level non-volatile repair switches heal failed hybrid bonds
idea: Eliminate scrapping stacks for a few bad vertical connections: place tiny ReRAM/antifuse crosspoint switches beside every 16 hybrid-bond pads plus 2 spares, programmed after post-bond test to route around opens and shorts; routing persists without power or e-fuse reload.
why: At 1-3 um pitch with millions of bonds, bond defects dominate stack yield; per-group sparing pushes vertical-link yield >99.9%, attacking the 20-30% HBM yield loss.

title: Helium-free laser-etched vias for memory stacks
idea: Scarcity: no helium (Qatar offline), so no He backside-cooled DRIE chucks and no He leak tests. Form through-vias by femtosecond laser modification plus selective wet etching (laser-induced deep etching) in glass or silicon carriers, and check hermeticity with a hydrogen/forming-gas tracer.
why: Helium chokepoint and via cost: batch wet etch handles many wafers per bath with no plasma tool, removing helium from via formation.

title: Wavelength-addressed banks: color selects the bank, not a decoder
idea: Invert 'addresses are decoded electrically in the periphery': each bank group gets a microring drop filter tuned to its own wavelength on a base-die waveguide bus, so a request on lambda-7 physically reaches only bank 7 and data returns on the same color; bank select becomes optical routing with no global address decode tree.
why: Attacks periphery (~49% of die) and global-wire energy; with comb lasers, 16-32 colors x 32 Gb/s per stack at ~1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM.

title: Pulse-position one-hot coding: one wire toggle carries eight bits
idea: Interconnect energy is paid per transition, not per bit. On wide hybrid-bond buses where wires are cheap, send each byte by toggling exactly one of 256 wires (position = value), or 1 of 16 wires in 1 of 16 time slots; edge-detecting receivers decode. Random NRZ spends ~4 transitions per byte, this spends 1.
why: ~4x fewer charge events per bit on die-to-die links (fact 5); multiplies with low-swing gains.

title: PON burst-mode PHY: memory links that sleep between bursts
idea: Fiber-to-the-home ONUs transmit in bursts with receivers that lock in tens of ns. Give memory PHYs burst-mode clock-data recovery with short preambles and ~1-5 ns wake, so termination, clocks and CDR are fully off between transactions instead of idling.
why: Memory links average 20-40% utilization yet burn much of their power idle; burst mode makes link energy proportional to accesses, ~5-10x lower energy per access at low utilization.

title: Test first, wire last: liquid-metal rewiring of good dies
idea: Reverse wire-then-test: mount dies on a substrate under PDMS microchannels, and after electrical test inject gallium-indium liquid metal only into channels that join good dies and good channels to the host, then seal, so defective dies are simply never connected.
why: Yield and capital for multi-die memory modules, without known-good-die test cost; PDMS soft lithography is basic, best for wide buses at <=1 GHz.

title: Sense-amp-direct bonding: data exits each bank vertically, skipping global I/O
idea: Jump the data path from millimeter global I/O lines to micrometer vertical hops: each bank's sense-amp stripe carries its own fine-pitch hybrid-bond field to the logic die above, so column data leaves exactly where it is sensed. Column muxes, global data lines and the center-strip I/O block disappear.
why: On-die global data movement is a large slice of the 3-4 pJ/bit (fact 5) and of periphery (fact 7); ~40-60% lower access energy and ~10-15% die area returned to cells.

title: Asynchronous logic fixed: clockless 1-of-4 links inside the HBM stack
idea: Asynchronous design (Fulcrum, Handshake Solutions) failed because whole-chip async needed tools nobody had. Confine it to one hard IP block: the vertical links between HBM core dies and the base die use delay-insensitive 1-of-4 encoding with completion detection, so the stack needs no clock TSVs, DLLs or per-die clock trees and each die runs as fast as its process corner allows.
why: Data movement (fact 5): clock distribution and DLLs are ~20-40% of DRAM I/O power and standby current; removing them and their timing margins claims 25-35% lower in-stack I/O energy and better yield across corners.

title: Die passport: on-die non-volatile test history ends retesting
idea: Eliminate repeated testing at every packaging step: each memory die carries a small OTP/ReRAM log written at wafer sort, burn-in and post-bond test (bin, repair map, timing margins, weak rows), read by the stacker and later by the system.
why: Test is ~10-20% of memory cost and HBM retests dies several times; passports cut test time ~30-50%, and systems use the weak-row map to avoid extra refresh.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory vault on U.S. industrial gas
idea: Invert 'memory runs at room temperature beside compute': put DRAM sleds in a liquid-nitrogen bath from domestic air-separation plants next to the racks, linked optically; at 77 K leakage falls orders of magnitude and wire resistance ~5-7x.
why: Refresh nearly vanishes (16-33% of idle power), retention rises, and cold copper allows longer passive links at the same pJ/bit.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory pods with kT-scaled link swings
idea: Thermal noise and leakage both scale with temperature: at 77 K, kT drops 4x, copper resistivity ~7x and access-transistor leakage collapses. Immerse HBM-plus-accelerator modules in LN2 and redesign links for ~4x lower swing, longer unrepeated wires and lower threshold voltages, with refresh nearly eliminated.
why: ~2-4x link energy reduction plus refresh removal and a lower voltage floor (facts 3, 5, 10).

title: Composite-autoclave batch curing of hundreds of HBM stacks at once
idea: Pre-tack dies into stacks, vacuum-bag whole carriers like aerospace composite layups, and apply isostatic gas pressure and heat in an autoclave so hundreds of stacks bond in one cycle. Uniform pressure replaces serial thermocompression heads.
why: Thermocompression bonding at ~20 s per die limits HBM output; batch isostatic bonding claims ~50x throughput and less die cracking.

title: Loom: woven glass-fiber and microwire fabric interposer
idea: From a 'loom': glass fibers and 10 um insulated Cu microwires are woven on a textile loom into a fabric, resin-impregnated, and laser-opened at the pad sites. The fabric gives thousands of chiplet-to-chiplet links with zero lithography.
why: Capital intensity and CoWoS scarcity; could cut interposer cost ~10x, and textile looms are a U.S.-buildable tool base.

title: Nesting: legacy DRAM dies embedded inside the organic substrate under the GPU
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: use existing embedded-component substrate lines (already used for power modules and phone substrates) to bury thinned LPDDR/DDR4 dies inside the organic package core directly beneath the accelerator. The dies connect upward through ~100 um laser vias. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Data movement (fact 5) and capacity: adds 16-64 GB per package without shoreline or an interposer, at ~1-2 pJ/bit versus ~10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5 DIMMs.

title: XIP-style narrow serial DRAM chiplets for a bulk capacity tier
idea: $1 microcontrollers execute in place from 12-pin Octal-SPI/HyperRAM parts. Define a 12-16-pin high-speed serial DRAM chiplet for accelerator capacity tiers, ringed on cheap substrate, with a large logic-side cache hiding latency.
why: Pins and PHY area per GB drop ~5-10x vs DDR/HBM, so many cheap older-node DRAM dies add capacity without HBM's TSV and interposer costs.

title: Metronome: compiled deterministic DRAM schedule for AI inference
idea: Like a metronome: compile a model's entire memory access stream ahead of time into a fixed tape of activate, read, refresh and precharge commands that avoids bank conflicts and refresh collisions. An FPGA-with-HBM controller plays the tape back.
why: Raises HBM bandwidth utilization from ~60% to ~90%, about 1.5x more work per stack, so fewer stacks are needed.

title: Cortical folding: polyimide memory sheet folded into TSV-free stacks
idea: The cortex folds a thin sheet to fit a large area into a small skull. Oxide-TFT memory tiles are deposited directly on one continuous polyimide sheet with copper traces, tested flat, then folded accordion-style into a stack, so tier-to-tier wiring runs around the folds instead of through TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSVs, no stacked-bond yield loss, every tile tested before folding, and no silicon wafer; stacking cost falls sharply for a few mm of extra wire.

title: Neural-implant address-event bus for sparse tensors
idea: Neural implants with 1,000+ electrodes send spikes as address events, not frames, to stay within milliwatts. Store activations and KV in a sparse layout and run the link in address-event representation: only nonzero values with compressed coordinates cross the PHY, each event gating its own lane.
why: At 70-95% activation sparsity (ReLU, MoE, pruned models) bits moved per logical access fall ~3-10x; energy tracks information rather than tensor size.

title: Capillary self-assembly places hundreds of DRAM dies at once
idea: Po: chips swim to their sockets. One mask defines hydrophilic bond sites on the target wafer; water droplets pull hundreds of DRAM dies into sub-micron alignment in parallel before hybrid bonding.
why: Die-to-wafer bonding throughput up ~10x versus pick-and-place, cutting stacking cost and tool count.

title: Final CMP step doubles as bond activation, no plasma
idea: Combine CMP with surface activation: a tailored final-polish slurry (colloidal silica plus OH/amine terminating chemistry) leaves the SiCN or oxide bond face densely silanol-terminated and particle-free, and dies bond in-line within minutes, skipping the argon/N2 plasma activation chamber.
why: Hybrid-bond cost and rare-gas independence: removes a tool and queue-time limit, ~15-25% lower hybrid-bond module cost, enabling argon-free die-to-wafer HBM stacking.

title: Room-temperature nanowire-velcro bonding for DRAM stacks
idea: Po: joints are grown, not soldered. Electrodeposit dense Cu nanowire forests on both bond faces; pressing them together interlocks the wires into a conductive mechanical joint at room temperature, avoiding reflow or 300-400 C anneals.
why: Protects DRAM retention (leakage tail) from thermal budget and allows ~3 um pitch and rework, cutting stack yield loss.

title: Generative weight seeds expanded on the memory base die
idea: Invert 'needed bytes must be stored and moved verbatim': store weights as a PRNG seed plus a low-rank or quantized residual, and let a base-die engine regenerate the full tensor on demand as it streams to the GPU.
why: If 50-80% of weight information folds into seeds plus residual, DRAM capacity and link traffic for weights drop 2-5x, stretching scarce bits.

title: Film-editing proxies: fetch most-significant bit-planes first, refine on demand
idea: Adapted from VFX proxy editing and progressive JPEG: tensors are stored as bit-planes in separate DRAM rows. The accelerator fetches the top 4-8 bits first and requests lower planes only for values whose contribution matters (e.g., large attention scores).
why: Overfetch and data movement (facts 5, 8): ~30-60% fewer bits moved for inference at the same accuracy.

title: Silicon LEDs failed on efficiency; SPAD receivers make them enough
idea: Silicon light emitters were abandoned for links because indirect-gap emission is 1e-5 efficient or worse. Across bonded dies (<20 um of oxide), a receiver built from silicon single-photon avalanche diodes needs only ~20-50 photons per bit, so a reverse-biased avalanche-mode Si junction, emitting fast 600-900 nm hot-carrier light, can signal die-to-die with no III-V, Ge or In.
why: Data movement with zero banned elements: a contactless, crosstalk-free optical die-to-die link needing no bumps; ~1-5 pJ/bit at first, limited honestly by emitter efficiency.

title: Function-shipping packets: memory requests carry bytecode run at the hub
idea: Invert the scale of what moves: instead of hauling gigabytes to the CPU, each CXL request carries a ~64-byte verified bytecode (filter, gather, reduce) that a tiny core on the memory hub executes, returning only the result. The fabric moves kernels, not data.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) drops 10-100x for gather and scan-heavy work, and fewer bits in flight shrink the DRAM needed for staging buffers.

title: Log-raft capillary self-assembly of DRAM dies onto logic wafers
idea: Drop DRAM dies onto water droplets confined by hydrophilic pad islands on a logic wafer; surface tension pulls each die into alignment within 0.5 um in under a second, like logs self-aligning in a river raft. The water then evaporates and a hybrid bond forms.
why: Attacks die-to-wafer bonding throughput (pick-and-place is the HBM bottleneck); claims ~10x faster placement at better alignment.

title: Exponent-plane storage: base die dedups bf16 exponents
idea: Ideal: store only information, never redundancy. Closest achievable: the HBM base die transparently splits bf16/fp8 tensors into sign-mantissa planes and an exponent plane, entropy-codes the low-entropy exponents (~2.5 bits instead of 8) and reassembles them at line rate on read.
why: Usable capacity and bandwidth: ~25-30% more effective HBM capacity and interface bandwidth for AI tensors with no host changes; fewer bits moved per useful value (fact 5).

title: Pool every switch FIFO and retimer buffer into network memory
idea: Worsen: let every switch, retimer and NIC hold its own idle SRAM FIFOs. Flip: expose the tens of MB of SRAM buffering in a rack's switches and CXL retimers as an addressable, latency-tagged pool for in-flight tensors, so data in transit lands in the network instead of DRAM.
why: Usable memory: reclaims stranded SRAM (GBs per rack) for collective and staging buffers and avoids DRAM round trips.

title: Astronomy CCD correlated double sampling enables 20 mV memory links
idea: Astronomical CCDs read single electrons by correlated double sampling, subtracting a reset sample from the signal sample. Put clocked CDS receivers on interposer/TSV links so offsets and low-frequency noise cancel, allowing 20-30 mV swings driven from a dedicated switched-capacitor 0.1 V rail.
why: Line energy ~C*Vswing*Vrail: 30 mV swing from a 0.1 V rail vs 0.4 V links cuts wire energy >10x, attacking data-movement energy and the voltage floor at the interface.

title: Bookshelf memory: dies stand on edge atop compute
idea: Eliminate both the interposer and TSVs: route top-metal lines to a polished, metallized die edge carrying ~2 um-pitch pads, stand dozens of DRAM dies vertically on the GPU's top surface and hybrid-bond their edges; the gaps between the standing dies become microfluidic coolant channels, so the memory doubles as a heat-sink fin array.
why: A 10 mm x 100 um edge offers ~250k contacts per die (more than a whole HBM stack) with zero TSV area and no interposer; vertical wire length <100 um targets <0.3 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM and attacks the TSV tax.

title: Books-on-a-shelf: DRAM dies standing edge-on over logic
idea: Po: the stack lies on its side. Stand thinned DRAM dies upright like books, each bonded along one polished edge carrying fine-pitch pads to the logic die beneath, with coolant flowing in the gaps between dies.
why: No TSVs and no stack height limit; every die is cooled directly and wired straight to logic, raising capacity per package without the TSV tax.

title: Spatially pipelined chiplet mesh: activations never land in memory
idea: Intermediate buffers exist only because producer and consumer run at different times. Map each layer group onto its own chiplet in a panel-scale mesh and chain them with FIFOs sized to pipeline skew, so activations flow directly chiplet to chiplet and activation DRAM goes to near zero.
why: Activation memory falls >100x; trades reconfigurability and needs many chiplets.

title: Car platform sharing: one DRAM core die, swappable interface chiplets
idea: Adapted from VW's shared MQB platform: fabs make one memory-array core die with a dense hybrid-bond face, and a separate interface chiplet turns it into DDR5, LPDDR, GDDR or HBM. Capacity moves between markets by changing only the cheap chiplet.
why: Capital and periphery (facts 4, 7): fewer mask sets, periphery moved to a cheaper logic node, and wafer starts reallocated in weeks, not quarters, during HBM/DDR shortages.

title: Memory-side top-k gate returns token indices, not keys
idea: Eliminate shipping full key vectors: each HBM pseudo-channel's base-die slice holds a small dot-product unit and comparator tree that scores the query against stored keys inside the stack and returns only the top-k token indices; only those value rows then cross the interface.
why: Long-context KV reads dominate decode bandwidth; for k=64 of 128k tokens interface traffic falls >10x for ~3-5% base-die area.

title: Thirteenth-die hot spare rescues HBM stack yield
idea: Eliminate 'one bad die scraps the stack': build 12-high stacks with a 13th identical spare die and a vertical channel crossbar in the base die; after final stack test, a failing die's channels are steered onto the spare.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30%: with 97% per-die post-bond survival, stack yield rises from ~69% (0.97^12) to ~94% with one spare, cutting effective cost/bit ~25%.

title: Telephone hybrid echo cancellation doubles bandwidth per memory pin
idea: Adapted from the 2-wire telephone hybrid and V.34/1000BASE-T echo cancellers: reads and writes travel on the same wire at the same moment, and each end subtracts its own transmitted signal using 180 nm analog circuits.
why: Pin and TSV count (facts 6, 7): 2x bandwidth per pin, or half the pins/TSVs for the same bandwidth, making up for slower old-node lanes.

title: Shape-memory alloy clamps that release chiplets at 80 C
idea: MINIFY disassembly effort: NiTi clamps hold memory chiplets on pressure contacts and spring open when the package is heated to ~80 C in a recycling oven, so dies drop out intact.
why: Recyclability with zero labor: separates dies, substrate and lid automatically for reuse or pure material streams.
